content: # How to write a talk

This guide takes you from the tour a new deck opens on to a talk you can present: where to write, how to build a slide, and how to check and show the result. It assumes the deck runs, as [Setup in the README](../README.md#setup) describes. The README is the reference for every component and option named here.
## Open the deck
Start the dev server:
```sh
pnpm dev
Open the address it prints, http://localhost:5173 unless that port is taken. The whole talk is one file, `slides.mdx`, at the root of the repository, and every save updates the slide on screen.
## Replace the tour

A new deck opens on a tour of what it can do. Page through it once with <kbd>→</kbd>, then replace everything in `slides.mdx` with your talk. When nothing includes them any more, delete `chapters/example.mdx` and `snippets/counter.ts`, the chapter and the sample code the tour uses. Git keeps the tour in the scaffold commit if you want to look at it again.
## Outline the talk first

Settle three things before you write a slide: who the audience is, how long you have (about one content slide a minute), and the one sentence you want the room to remember. Then write every slide's headline, in order, before any slide's body, and read the headlines as a paragraph. If they do not make your argument on their own, no slide body will.
## Write a slide

The frontmatter at the top of `slides.mdx` sets the deck's title, and a line of `---` with a blank line before it starts each new slide. This is a talk of two slides, a cover and one claim with its evidence, in `slides.mdx`:
```mdx
title: "Caching the catalogue"
<Cover>
# Caching the catalogue
A week of cache misses, and what fixed them
</Cover>
## Caching cut p99 latency from 800 ms to 120 ms
<Stat value="120 ms" label="p99 latency with the cache, down from 800 ms" />
<Notes>
- Measured over the week of 12 March on the production dashboard
- The cache holds the 2,000 most-read products
</Notes>
Each content slide follows the same rules:
- The `##` headline states the slide's claim as a sentence of at most two lines, not a topic such as "Results".
- The body is the evidence for it: code, a diagram, one number in `<Stat>`, a table, an image, or two things side by side in `<Columns>`.
- The slide holds about 20 words you can see, and a list holds at most four items.
- What you will say goes in `<Notes>`, which the presenter view shows and the audience never sees.
`<Cover>`, `<Section>`, `<Statement>` and `<Quote>` fill a whole slide: use them to open, to start a new part, for a line to remember, and to close.
## Reveal a slide in steps

Wrap a list in `<Steps>` to reveal one item per press of <kbd>→</kbd>, or a block in `<Step>` to reveal it on the next press. Code steps through highlights: `{1|3-4|all}` after a fence's language lights those lines, one set per step, and a highlight inside a fold opens it.
The overview and the printed deck show every slide fully revealed, so end each slide on a step that makes sense alone. For code, that means ending on `all`.
## Add code and diagrams

A fenced code block is highlighted when the deck builds. Give it `title="src/app.ts"` for a title bar, `diff` to show a change, or `file="./snippets/app.ts#setup"` to show a region of a real file, which `pnpm typecheck` keeps compiling. A `mermaid` fence becomes a diagram drawn in the deck's colours. [Code blocks](../README.md#code-blocks) and [Diagrams](../README.md#diagrams) in the README list every option.

Code has to fit at full size. While `pnpm dev` runs, a slide says so in its top corner when it does not: cut the code, fold what is not the point with `fold={4-11}`, split the slide, or give the fence `maxLines=10` to scroll it. Never make the text smaller.
## Split a long talk into files
To keep a long talk manageable, move each part into its own file under `chapters/`, written like `slides.mdx`, and include it where it belongs. In `slides.mdx`:
```mdx
<Include src="./chapters/results.mdx" />
## Check every slide
Run the check before you rehearse, and again before you present:
```sh
pnpm check

It type-checks the slides, builds the deck and renders every step of every slide. It fails on content that runs off a slide or out of a code frame, and warns about code or a diagram shrunk to fit; fix both. The images it writes to `.tmp/export/` show each slide fully revealed, as the room will see it, so read the headlines there in order once more.
## Present and share

With `pnpm dev` running, open the deck in the browser you present from and press <kbd>F</kbd> for full screen. Press <kbd>P</kbd> to open the presenter view in a window of its own, with your notes, the next slide and a timer, and keep that window on your screen. <kbd>→</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd> or a clicker's Page Down moves on, and <kbd>?</kbd> lists every shortcut.
To hand the deck out, `pnpm export` writes `.tmp/export/slides.pdf`, a page per slide. To publish it, `pnpm build` writes `dist/`, a static site that any host serves, under any path.
## Write with an agent

Coding agents working in this repository load the `writing-slides` skill from `.agents/skills/writing-slides/` when you ask them to write, shorten, restructure or review the talk. It holds the rules this guide summarises, with the measured limits, and it runs `pnpm check` before it finishes. Its references are worth reading yourself: `talk-structure.md` on the arc and the timing, `code-slides.md` on how much code fits, and `failure-modes.md` on what goes wrong most often.
